claim: Plasmodium falciparum remains one of the leading causes of mortality among children under 5 years of age.
source: Despite progress made to reduce the global malaria burden, Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) remains one of the leading causes of mortality among children under 5 years of age (Geneva: World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization 2022 report

claim: Progress in malaria control has plateaued since 2015.
source: Unfortunately, progress has been impeded by a plateau in malaria control since 2015.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the introduction

claim: Malaria cases in children under 5 years of age increased from 17.6 million in 2015 to 19.2 million in 2021 in East and Southern African countries.
source: Antimalarial drug resistance (Taylor and Juliano, 2014; Aydemir et al., 2018) and unprecedented logistical challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic that dramatically impacted the distribution of insecticide-impregnated mosquito nets led to an increase in malaria cases in children under 5 years of age from 17.6 million in 2015 to 19.2 million in 2021 in East and Southern African countries (Geneva: World Health Organization, 2022; Ippolito et al., 2021), thus, contributing to reinvigorated prioritization of malaria vaccine initiatives.
evidence: Supported by citations to WHO 2022 and Ippolito et al., 2021

claim: RTS,S/AS01E was the first malaria vaccine approved by the World Health Organization in 2021.
source: After 30 years of development, the first malaria vaccine—RTS,S/AS01E—was approved by the World Health Organization in 2021 for use in children residing in malaria-endemic regions.
evidence: Stated as a fact about vaccine approval

claim: RTS,S has limited efficacy, particularly against severe malaria.
source: However, the limited efficacy of RTS,S, (RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015) particularly against severe malaria (RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015), has motivated the search for additional vaccine candidate antigens, including blood-stage Pf-schizont egress antigen-1 (PfSEA-1A) (Raj et al., 2014) and Pf-glutamic acid-rich protein (PfGARP) (Raj et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015

claim: Antibodies against PfSEA-1A correlate with significantly lower parasite densities in Kenyan adults and adolescents.
source: Antibodies against PfSEA-1A correlate with significantly lower parasite densities in Kenyan adults and adolescents and substantially reduce schizont replication in vitro (Raj et al., 2014; Nixon et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Raj et al., 2014 and Nixon et al., 2017

claim: PfGARP-specific antibodies kill trophozoite-infected erythrocytes in culture.
source: whereas PfGARP-specific antibodies kill trophozoite-infected erythrocytes in culture and confer partial protection against Pf challenge in vaccinated nonhuman primates (Raj et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raj et al., 2020

claim: The presence of antibodies against PfGARP was associated with a 2-fold-lower parasite density in Kenyan adults and adolescents.
source: The presence of antibodies against PfGARP was associated with a 2-fold-lower parasite density in Kenyan adults and adolescents (Raj et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raj et al., 2020

claim: A multivalent vaccine would be more efficacious against malaria due to the complexity of the parasite's life cycle.
source: Due to the complexity of the parasites' life cycle, there is general agreement that a multivalent vaccine would be more efficacious (Holder, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holder, 1999

claim: Antigen-specific CD4pos T-follicular helper (TFH) cells are required to provide cellular and molecular signals to trigger B-cell proliferation.
source: Affinity maturation takes place in the germinal center (GC), where antigen-specific CD4pos T-follicular helper (TFH) cells are required not only to provide cellular (CD40L) and molecular (IL-21, IL-4, and IL-13) signals to trigger B-cell proliferation but also to promote GC maintenance and plasmablast differentiation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TFH cell function

claim: CXCR5 directs CD4pos T cells from the T-cell zone to engage with follicular B cells.
source: TFH cells are defined by the expression of a combination of markers, starting with chemokine receptor CXCR5, which directs CD4pos T cells from the T-cell zone to engage with follicular B cells (Breitfeld et al., 2000; Crotty, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Breitfeld et al., 2000 and Crotty, 2011

claim: Circulating TFH (cTFH) cells correlate with the generation of long-lasting antibody responses.
source: Once antigen-experienced TFH cells leave the GC, they become circulating TFH (cTFH) cells and correlate with the generation of long-lasting antibody responses.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about cTFH cells

claim: cTFH cells can originate from peripheral cTFH precursor CCR7lowPD1highCXCR5pos cells, indicating a GC-independent origin.
source: Interestingly, cTFH cells can also come from peripheral cTFH precursor CCR7lowPD1highCXCR5pos cells; thus, they also have a GC-independent origin (He et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to He et al., 2013

claim: cTFH cells are categorized into subsets based on CCR6 and CXCR3 expression: cTFH1 (CCR6negCXCR3pos), cTFH2 (CCR6negCXCR3neg), and cTFH17 (CCR6posCXCR3neg).
source: Expression profiles of CCR6 and CXCR3 further categorize cTFH into subsets as follows: cTFH1 (CCR6negCXCR3pos), cTFH2 (CCR6negCXCR3neg), and cTFH17 (CCR6posCXCR3neg) (Schmitt et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmitt et al., 2014

claim: Bcl6 facilitates the production of IL-21 by T cells, which aids B-cell affinity maturation and antibody production.
source: Bcl6 facilitates the production of IL-21 by T cells, which aids B-cell affinity maturation and antibody production (Nurieva et al., 2009; Nurieva and Chung, 2010; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nurieva et al., 2009; Nurieva and Chung, 2010; Liu et al., 2013

claim: In Mali, TH1-polarized cTFH PD1posCXCR5posCXCR3pos cells were preferentially activated in children and less efficient than CXCR3neg cTFH cells in helping autologous B cells to produce antibodies.
source: In Mali, where malaria is seasonal, Obeng-Adjei and colleagues showed that TH1-polarized cTFH PD1posCXCR5posCXCR3pos cells were preferentially activated in children and less efficient than CXCR3neg cTFH cells in helping autologous B cells to produce antibodies; yet they used US healthy adult cTFH cells for their in vitro assays.
evidence: Supported by reference to Obeng-Adjei and colleagues' work

claim: In Papua, Indonesia, all cTFH subsets from adults showed higher activation and proliferation status compared to cTFH cells from children.
source: Similarly, a study in Papua, Indonesia, where malaria is perennial, found that all cTFH subsets from adults showed higher activation and proliferation status compared to cTFH cells from children (Oyong et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oyong et al., 2022

claim: In Uganda, a shift from TH2- to TH1-polarized cTFH subsets occurred during the first 6 years of life and was associated with the development of functional antibodies against Pf-malaria.
source: One study in Uganda, where malaria is holoendemic with seasonal peaks, showed that a shift from TH2- to TH1-polarized cTFH subsets occurred during the first 6 years of life and was associated with the development of functional antibodies against Pf-malaria, yet appeared to be independent of malaria exposure and this age-associated shift was also observed in a malaria-naïve population (Chan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 2022

claim: A higher proportion of TH17-cTFH cells was associated with a decreased risk of Pf infection the following year in Uganda.
source: Interestingly, this study also found that a higher proportion of TH17-cTFH cells was associated with a decreased risk of Pf infection the following year; however, the authors postulated that this phenomenon could have been driven by the previous exposure to the parasite.
evidence: Supported by reference to the Uganda study

claim: Children had significantly lower median level of IgG against PfSEA-1A compared to adults.
source: We found that children had a significantly lower median level of IgG against PfSEA-1A, compared to adults (p<0.0001), whereas median levels to PfGARP were similarly high for adults and children, yet with a broad range of reactivity.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1b showing statistical comparison

claim: Median levels of IgG to PfGARP were similarly high for adults and children.
source: We found that children had a significantly lower median level of IgG against PfSEA-1A, compared to adults (p<0.0001), whereas median levels to PfGARP were similarly high for adults and children, yet with a broad range of reactivity.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1b

claim: No statistical difference was observed in absolute lymphocyte count between children and adults.
source: No statistical difference was observed (p=0.35 after Welch's test) regarding the absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) between children (mean of 373.1; standard deviation [SD] of 118.1) and adults (mean of 335.2; SD of 99.08).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results (Welch's test, p=0.35)

claim: Children had significantly lower hematocrit values compared to adults.
source: Children had significantly lower hematocrit values (median of 37%, interquartile range [IQR] of 32.7–40.5) compared to adults (median of 44.4%, IQR of 40.5–46), p=0.002 after a two-tailed Mann-Whitney t-test; however, these values were within normal ranges after adjusting for age (Pluncevic Gligoroska et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results (Mann-Whitney t-test, p=0.002) and citation

claim: All study participants had high IgG levels against merozoite antigens AMA-1 and MSP1, confirming at least one Pf-infection within their lifetime.
source: All participants had high IgG levels against merozoite antigens, apical membrane antigen 1 (AMA-1), and merozoite surface protein (MSP1), confirming at least one Pf-infection within their lifetime (Yman et al., 2019; O'Flaherty et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1a and citations to Yman et al., 2019 and O'Flaherty et al., 2021

claim: Overall abundances of cTFH cells were similar across conditions for both adults and children after 6 hr stimulation.
source: As expected, after a short stimulation (6 hr), overall abundances of cTFH cells were similar across conditions for both adults (Figure 2b) and children (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2b and 2c

claim: In vitro stimulation did not preferentially expand any of the T-cell populations.
source: This observation was confirmed by EdgeR statistical analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and demonstrated that in vitro stimulation did not preferentially expand any of the T-cell populations on which we based our subsequent analyses.
evidence: Supported by EdgeR statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Activated PD1high cTFH1or2-like (MC03), activated cTFH1-like (MC06), and quiescent ICOShigh cTFH1or2-like (MC08) subsets were significantly more abundant in children compared to adults regardless of stimulation conditions.
source: We found that activated PD1high cTFH1or2-like (MC03), activated cTFH1-like (MC06), and quiescent ICOShigh cTFH1or2-like (MC08) subsets were significantly more abundant in children compared to adults regardless of the stimulation conditions (Figure 5b, c, and d, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5b, c, and d with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: The quiescent PfSEA-1A- and PfGARP-specific cTFH2-like cluster (MC02) was significantly more abundant in adults compared to children.
source: In contrast, the quiescent PfSEA-1A- and PfGARP-specific cTFH2-like cluster (MC02) was significantly more abundant in adults compared to children (Figure 5c and d, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5c and d with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: Following PfGARP stimulation, the activated cTFH1/17-like subset (MC09) became more abundant in children compared to adults.
source: Interestingly, following PfGARP stimulation, the activated cTFH1/17-like subset (MC09) became more abundant in children compared to adults (Figure 5d, p<0.05 with a false discovery rate [FDR] = 0.08), but no additional subsets shifted phenotype after PfSEA-1A stimulation (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5d with statistical significance p<0.05 and FDR=0.08

claim: PfSEA-1A and PfGARP induced robust IL-4 expression in 9 out of 12 cTFH meta-clusters in children.
source: For children, PfSEA-1A and PfGARP induced robust IL-4 expression in 9 out of 12 cTFH meta-clusters (p-values≤0.0105); although the composition of which cTFH subsets were engaged differed slightly by antigen (quiescent cTFH1or2-like ICOSlow MC05 vs quiescent cTFH2-like MC02, respectively).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-values≤0.0105

claim: No change in expression for IFNγ or IL-21 was observed after in vitro antigen stimulation in children.
source: In contrast to IL-4, we observed no change in expression for IFNγ or IL-21 after in vitro antigen stimulation (except for quiescent cTFH1or2-like ICOShigh MC08, p-value=0.0391), suggesting that these cytokines are not informative to define the development of antigen-specific cTFH subsets in children.
evidence: Based on observation of expression data with one exception

claim: PfGARP induced significantly more Bcl6 expression within activated and quiescent cTFH2-like subsets (MC01 and MC02) as well as activated PD1high cTFH1or2-like (MC03) cells compared to PfSEA-1A stimulation in children.
source: In Group 1, Bcl6 expression was significantly higher within activated and quiescent cTFH2-like subsets (MC01 and MC02) as well as activated PD1high cTFH1or2-like (MC03) cells after PfGARP compared to PfSEA-1A stimulation (p=0.0266, p=0.0134, and p=0.0327, respectively, Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with specific p-values and Figure 6e

claim: PfGARP induced IFNγ and Bcl6 expression by activated cTFH1-like (MC06) cells at higher levels compared to PfSEA-1A stimulation in children.
source: Within Group 2, IFNγ and Bcl6 were highly expressed by activated cTFH1-like (MC06) after PfGARP stimulation compared to PfSEA-1A stimulation (p=0.0093 and p=0.0024, respectively, Figure 6c and e).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with specific p-values and Figure 6c and e

claim: Activated cTFH1/17-like cells (MC11) expressed higher cMAF after PfSEA-1A stimulation compared to PfGARP in children.
source: Finally, within Group 3, the activated cTFH1/17-like cells (MC11) expressed higher cMAF after PfSEA-1A stimulation compared to PfGARP (p=0.0186, Figure 6f).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with p=0.0186 and Figure 6f

claim: PfSEA-1A and PfGARP induced significant expression of both IFNγ and IL-4 for activated (MC01) and quiescent (MC02) cTFH2-like cells in adults.
source: Here, we found that both PfSEA-1A and PfGARP induced significant expression of both IFNγ and IL-4 for activated (MC01) and quiescent (MC02) cTFH2-like cells (Figure 7a and b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7a, 7b, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: PfGARP induced IL-4 and IFNγ expression from quiescent and activated cTFH17-like cells (MC10 and MC13) in adults.
source: Whereas PfGARP also induced IL-4 and IFNγ expression from quiescent and activated cTFH17-like cells (MC10 and MC13), in addition to Bcl6 and cMAF for MC13 (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: Activated cTFH1/17-like cells (MC11) only responded to PfGARP in adults, expressing higher levels of IL-4, IL-21, Bcl6, and cMAF.
source: In contrast, activated the cTFH1/17-like cells (MC11) only responded to PfGARP (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), expressing higher levels of IL-4, IL-21, Bcl6, and cMAF.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: PfGARP induced more Bcl6 expression than PfSEA-1A within the quiescent cTFH2-like subset (MC02) in adults.
source: Finally, while assessing the differences between the two malaria antigens, we found that PfGARP induced more Bcl6 expression than PfSEA-1A within the quiescent cTFH2-like subset (MC02, p=0.0327) and the quiescent ICOSlow cTFH1or2-like cells (MC05, p=0.0105), as well as within the quiescent cTFH17-like subset (MC10, p=0.0479) and the activated cTFH1/17-like cells (MC11, p=0.0020) (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with p=0.0327 and Figure 7d

claim: An activated cTFH1or2-like subset (MC04) was more abundant in participants with high levels of anti-PfGARP IgG for both children and adults after PfGARP stimulation.
source: When stratifying by high vs low anti-PfGARP IgG antibody levels, we found that an activated cTFH1or2-like subset (MC04) was more abundant in participants with high levels of anti-PfGARP IgG for both children (Figure 8a) and adults (Figure 8b) after PfGARP stimulation compared to participants with low levels or an absence of anti-PfGARP IgG.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8a and 8b

claim: Activated cTFH1-like (MC06) and quiescent cTFH1-like (MC07) cells were more abundant for adults with low or no anti-PfGARP IgG antibodies compared to those with high levels.
source: Interestingly, activated cTFH1-like (MC06) and quiescent cTFH1-like (MC07) cells were more abundant for adults with low or no anti-PfGARP IgG antibodies compared to those with high levels (p=0.0024 with FDR = 0.0185 and p=0.0034 with FDR = 0.0185, respectively), consistent with previous observations describing TFH1 subsets as inefficient help for antibody production (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with specific p-values and FDR, and citation to Obeng-Adjei et al., 2015

claim: Children not only respond via their cTFH1-like subsets but also engage a broader spectrum of cTFH subsets.
source: Contrary to the previous publications (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2015; Oyong et al., 2022), our study found that children not only respond via their cTFH1-like subsets but also engage a broader spectrum of cTFH subsets.
evidence: Based on the study's findings and comparison to previous publications

claim: In adults, the dominant antigen-specific memory response was from cTFH17- and cTFH1/17-like subsets but only for PfGARP.
source: In fact, cytokine and transcription factor profiles for children involved cTFH1-, cTFH2-, cTFH17-, and cTFH1/17-like subsets (summarized in Figure 9), whereas in adults, the dominant antigen-specific memory response was from cTFH17- and cTFH1/17-like subsets but only for PfGARP.
evidence: Based on the study's findings summarized in Figure 9

claim: TFH17 cells are involved in the maintenance of memory antibody responses within the context of parasitic infections.
source: Because TFH17 cells are involved in the maintenance of memory antibody responses within the context of parasitic infections, our results suggest that PfGARP might generate longer-lived antibody responses compared to PfSEA-1A.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TFH17 cells

claim: PfGARP might generate longer-lived antibody responses compared to PfSEA-1A.
source: Because TFH17 cells are involved in the maintenance of memory antibody responses within the context of parasitic infections, our results suggest that PfGARP might generate longer-lived antibody responses compared to PfSEA-1A.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings about TFH17 cell responses to PfGARP

claim: Antibody levels appear to be unreliable predictors of malaria vaccine efficacy.
source: Antibody levels appear to be unreliable predictors of malaria vaccine efficacy (Stanisic and McCall, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stanisic and McCall, 2021

claim: cMAF cooperates with Bcl6 in TFH development and function and is essential to establish an efficient GC response.
source: Importantly, cMAF cooperates with Bcl6 in TFH development and function and is essential to establish an efficient GC response (Nurieva et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nurieva et al., 2009 and Yu et al., 2009

claim: PfGARP induced a highly significant increase of Bcl6 in cTFH2-like and cTFH17-like subsets in children, suggesting that PfGARP may be a better candidate to trigger an efficient humoral response in children compared to PfSEA-1A.
source: In our study, PfGARP induced a highly significant increase of Bcl6 in cTFH2-like and cTFH17-like subsets in children, suggesting that PfGARP may be a better candidate to trigger an efficient humoral response in children compared to PfSEA-1A.
evidence: Based on the study's findings and inference about vaccine candidate potential

claim: Study participants did not have blood-stage malaria infections at the time of blood collection.
source: Study participants did not have blood-stage malaria infections at the time of blood collection, and children were 7 years of age; thus, our profiles were by design meant to reflect cTFH memory recall responses and demonstrate differences between children and adults.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study design

claim: The study used spectral flow cytometry and unbiased clustering analysis to assess antigen-specific cTFH cell recall responses.
source: Using spectral flow cytometry and unbiased clustering analysis, we assessed antigen-specific cTFH cell recall responses in vitro to malaria vaccine candidates Pf-schizont egress antigen-1 (PfSEA-1A) and Pf-glutamic acid-rich protein (PfGARP) within a cross-section of children and adults living in a malaria-holoendemic region of western Kenya.
evidence: Stated as the study methodology

claim: The study included 7-year-old children and adults with a mean age of 22.67 years (ranging from 19 to 30 years of age).
source: This cross-sectional study selected a convenience sample of 7-year-old children and adults with a mean age of 22.67 years (ranging from 19 to 30 years of age).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study population

claim: The study was conducted in a malaria-holoendemic region of Western Kenya.
source: Using spectral flow cytometry and unbiased clustering analysis, we assessed antigen-specific cTFH cell recall responses in vitro to malaria vaccine candidates Pf-schizont egress antigen-1 (PfSEA-1A) and Pf-glutamic acid-rich protein (PfGARP) within a cross-section of children and adults living in a malaria-holoendemic region of western Kenya.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study location

claim: The study used a 6-hour in vitro stimulation assay.
source: As expected, after a short stimulation (6 hr), overall abundances of cTFH cells were similar across conditions for both adults (Figure 2b) and children (Figure 2c).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study methodology

claim: The study identified 12 distinct cTFH meta-clusters using FlowSOM unbiased clustering analysis.
source: Based on CXCR3 and CCR6 expressions as well as the expression of effector/memory/activation markers (CCR7, CD127, PD1, and ICOS), cytokines (IFNγ, IL-4, and IL-21), and transcription factors (Bcl6 and cMAF), we initially identified 15 meta-clusters within the CD4posCXCR5pos T cells (Figure 3a).
evidence: Based on the study's analysis methodology and results shown in Figure 3a

claim: Three meta-clusters (MC12, MC14, and MC15) were excluded because they were likely naïve cells with transient low expression of CXCR5 and high expression of CD45RA.
source: Because CD45RAposCXCR5pos cells are likely naïve cells with transient low expression of CXCR5, yet high expression of CD45RA, we excluded three meta-clusters using these criteria (i.e. MC12, MC14, and MC15) (Figure 3c).
evidence: Based on the study's analysis criteria and results shown in Figure 3c

claim: The most common cTFH subset in both children and adults was the quiescent cTFH2-like cells (MC02, 24.1% and 41.2%, respectively).
source: Overall, the most common cTFH subset in both children and adults was the quiescent cTFH2-like cells (MC02, 24.1% and 41.2%, respectively).
evidence: Based on the study's quantitative analysis of cTFH subset abundance

claim: The activated PD1low cTFH1or2-like cells (MC04) were less abundant in children with low compared to high HRP2 antibody levels.
source: Of note, only the activated PD1low cTFH1or2-like cells (MC04) were less abundant in children with low compared to high HRP2 antibody levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this subset may be involved in short-term antibody production.
evidence: Based on the study's analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: HRP2-specific antibodies are short-lived and could serve as a surrogate for a recent infection.
source: We observed a clear bimodal distribution in antibody levels against histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP2) with half of the children having 'high-HRP2' vs 'low-HRP2' IgG levels, possibly a reflection of recent malaria history since it has been suggested that HRP2-specific antibodies are short-lived and could serve as a surrogate for a recent infection (Turnbull et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turnbull et al., 2022

claim: The study used peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) isolated from study participants.
source: Venous blood was collected in sodium heparin BD Vacutainers and processed within 2 hr at the Center for Global Health Research, KEMRI, Kisumu. ALCs were determined from whole blood using the BC-3000 Plus Auto Hematology Analyzer, 19 parameters (Shenzhen Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics Co). After 10 min at 1000×g spin, plasma was removed and stored at –20°C, and an equivalent volume of 1× PBS was added to the cell pellet. PBMCs were then isolated using Ficoll-Hypaque density gradient centrifugation on SepMate (StemCell).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study methodology

claim: The study used a multiparameter spectral flow cytometry panel with 21 markers to characterize cTFH cell subsets.
source: A multiparameter spectral flow cytometry panel was used to characterize cTFH cell subsets: CCR6-BV421 (RRID:AB_2561356), CD14-Pacific Blue (RRID:AB_830689), CD19-Pacific Blue (RRID:AB_2073118), CCR7-BV480 (RRID:AB_2739502), IFNγ-BV510 (RRID:AB_2563883), CD127-BV570 (RRID:AB_10900064), CD45RA-BV605 (RRID:AB_2563814), PD1-BV650 (RRID:AB_2738746), CXCR3-BV711 (RRID:AB_2563533), CD25-BV750 (RRID:AB_2871896), CXCR5-BV785 (RRID:AB_2629528), Bcl6-AF488 (RRID:AB_10716202), CD3-Spark Blue 550 (RRID:AB_2819985), CD8-PerCP-Cy5.5 (RRID:AB_2044010), IL-21-PE (RRID:AB_2249025), IL-4-PE-Dazzle (RRID:AB_2564036), CD4-PE-Cy5 (RRID:AB_314078), ICOS-PE-Cy7 (RRID:AB_10643411), cMAF-eFluor 660 (RRID:AB_2574388), CD40L-AF700 (RRID:AB_2750053), and Zombie NIR (BioLegend cat# 423106) for Live/Dead staining.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study methodology

claim: The study received ethical approvals from the Scientific and Ethics Review Unit (SERU) at the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) and the Institutional Review Board at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School.
source: Ethical approvals were obtained from the Scientific and Ethics Review Unit (SERU) at the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) reference number 3542, and the Institutional Review Board at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA, USA, IRB number H00014522.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study's ethical approvals
